title: Setting Up Your Environment
description: Install .NET SDK and set up your development environment.

data.text: Before you can write and run C# code, you need to install the .NET Software Development Kit (SDK) and choose a code editor or Integrated Development Environment (IDE).
What is the .NET SDK?

The .NET SDK contains everything you need to build .NET applications: the C# compiler (`csc`), the `dotnet` CLI tool, the runtime, and the base class libraries. Without the SDK, you cannot compile C# code into runnable applications.

data.title: Choose the LTS Version
data.text: Always download the LTS (Long Term Support) version of .NET for production use. LTS versions receive security updates for three years and are more stable. The current LTS is .NET 8.0.
Installing .NET SDK
The installation process is straightforward on all major operating systems.

data.title: Windows Installation Steps
items: Select the .NET SDK (not just the Runtime)
Download the LTS version installer (e.g., .NET 8.0 SDK)
Run the installer and accept the license agreement
Verify installation by opening Command Prompt and running: dotnet --version

data.text: On macOS, you can use the native installer or install via Homebrew: `brew install --cask dotnet-sdk`. On Linux, use your distribution's package manager or follow the instructions on Microsoft's documentation.

data.title: Verify Your Installation
data.code:
dotnet --version
# Output: 8.0.100

dotnet --list-sdks
# Output: 8.0.100 [C:\Program Files\dotnet\sdk]

dotnet --list-runtimes

data.text: Code Editors and IDEs
C# development is supported by several excellent editors. Your choice depends on your OS, budget, and how many advanced features you want.

cards.title: Visual Studio 2022
cards.description: Microsoft's flagship IDE for Windows. The most feature-rich C# development environment available.

cards.title: Visual Studio Code
cards.description: Lightweight, cross-platform editor with excellent C# support via the C# Dev Kit extension.
cons: Less built-in than full Visual Studio

cards.title: JetBrains Rider
cards.description: Premium cross-platform IDE from JetBrains with deep C# and .NET support.
cons: Paid (with free trial and student licenses)

data.text: VS Code Setup (Recommended for Beginners)
Visual Studio Code with the C# Dev Kit extension is the recommended setup for beginners because it's free, lightweight, and works on any operating system.

items.text: Download and install VS Code from https://code.visualstudio.com
items.hint: Choose the installer for your operating system

items.text: Open VS Code and go to the Extensions view (Ctrl+Shift+X or Cmd+Shift+X)
items.hint: Click the Extensions icon in the left sidebar

items.text: Search for 'C# Dev Kit' by Microsoft and install it
items.hint: This provides IntelliSense, debugging, and project management
Some extensions require a restart to fully activate

items.text: Open a terminal in VS Code (Ctrl+`) and verify dotnet works

data.text: Creating and Running a Project
The .NET CLI (Command Line Interface) is a powerful tool for creating, building, and running .NET projects without an IDE.
Common .NET CLI Commands

data.title: Essential Commands
items: `dotnet new console -n MyApp` — Create a new console project named 'MyApp'
`dotnet run` — Build and run the project in the current directory
`dotnet build` — Compile the project without running it
`dotnet test` — Run unit tests in the project
`dotnet new sln -n MySolution` — Create a solution file to organize multiple projects
`dotnet new classlib -n MyLibrary` — Create a class library project

data.title: Create and Run Your First Project
data.content: Using the .NET CLI to create a console app
data.code:
# Create a new console application project
dotnet new console -n MyFirstApp

# Navigate into the project directory
cd MyFirstApp

# Run the application
dotnet run

# Output:
# Hello, World!

data.text: When you run `dotnet new console`, it creates a project file (`.csproj`) and a default `Program.cs` file with a simple Hello World program. The `dotnet run` command builds the project and immediately executes it.
Understanding Project Structure
A typical .NET console project has a simple structure. Understanding these files will help you navigate your project effectively.

data.title: Project Files
items: **Program.cs** — The main entry point of your application where top-level statements or the Main method lives
**MyFirstApp.csproj** — The project file that defines the project type, target framework, and dependencies
**bin/** and **obj/** — Build output directories generated automatically (do not edit)
**.sln** — Solution file (created when you add `dotnet new sln`), used to group multiple projects

data.content: A minimal .csproj file for a console app

data.title: SDK-Style Projects
data.text: Modern .NET uses SDK-style projects where most configuration is inferred. You rarely need to manually edit the .csproj file unless adding package references or changing the target framework.
Installing NuGet Packages
NuGet is the package manager for .NET. You can add third-party libraries to your project with the `dotnet add package` command.
The `dotnet add package` command downloads the package and adds it to your `.csproj` file. You can then use it in your C# code by adding an appropriate `using` statement.
Common Setup Issues

data.title: Troubleshooting
items: **'dotnet' is not recognized** — Restart your terminal after installing. On Windows, you may need to log out and back in.
**Wrong SDK version** — Run `dotnet --list-sdks` to see installed versions. Ensure your project's `<TargetFramework>` matches an installed SDK.
**VS Code IntelliSense not working** — Make sure the C# Dev Kit extension is installed and enabled. Check the Output panel for errors.
**Permission denied on macOS/Linux** — You may need to run `sudo dotnet ...` or ensure the dotnet directory has correct permissions.

data.title: Restart After Installation
data.text: After installing the .NET SDK, always close and reopen your terminal, VS Code, or IDE. This ensures the system PATH is updated and the `dotnet` command is available.

data.title: Exercise: Set Up Your Environment
data.description: Follow these steps to verify your development environment is ready.
steps: Install the .NET 8.0 (or latest LTS) SDK from Microsoft's website
Install VS Code with the C# Dev Kit extension
Open a terminal and run `dotnet --version` to confirm installation
Create a new console project with `dotnet new console -n SetupTest`
Navigate into the project folder with `cd SetupTest`
Run the project with `dotnet run` and see the Hello World output
Add the Humanizer NuGet package with `dotnet add package Humanizer`
Write code that uses Humanizer to pluralize a word (e.g., 'person' -> 'people')
data.expectedOutcome: You have a working .NET environment and can create, build, and run C# console applications with external packages.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: VS Code + C# Dev Kit is the recommended free, cross-platform setup
Use `dotnet new console -n Name` to create projects
Use `dotnet run` to build and run your project
Use `dotnet add package` to install NuGet packages
Always restart your terminal after installing the SDK
data.takeaway: With the SDK and an editor installed, you're ready to write real C# applications.
